title: 7. Increasing concentrate in lamb finishing diets improved feed efficiency and produced subtle effects on methane emissions.
content:
Abstract
Sheep are managed across a diverse range of production systems, from intensive confinement to extensive pasture-based operations, creating substantial variation in finishing diet composition potentially impacting methane emissions. The effects of varying dietary compositions on resource efficiency and environmental outcomes remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of three grain-to-forage ratios on feeder lamb growth, feed efficiency, and methane emissions. We hypothesized that increasing grain composition in the diet would improve animal growth rate, increase gain;feed, and reduce methane emissions as compared to diets with greater roughage inclusion. Commercial Rambouillet feeder lambs (N = 26) were stratified by initial bodyweight (BW; 58.1±4.14kg) and sex and randomly assigned to one of three ad libitum dietary treatments differing in grain-to-roughage ratio (GRR): high-grain (HG, 80:20 GRR; n = 7), mixed (MIX, 50:50 GRR; n = 10), or high-roughage (HR, 20:80 GRR; n = 9). Following a 14-d dietary treatment adaptation, lambs were adapted to 1 of 3 smart-feed intake monitoring systems (SmartFeed Pro, C-Lock Inc.) containing their respective dietary treatments to collect dry matter intake (DMI) and calculate gain:feed over a 35-d trial period. Six lambs failed to adequately adapt to the feed intake monitoring system and were removed. Lambs had unlimited access to an automatic head-chamber gas-capture system (GreenFeed, C-Lock Inc.) to estimate methane emissions throughout the 35-d trial period. Nineteen lambs (n = 5 HG; n = 6 MIX; n = 8 HR) met gas-capture system visitation thresholds and were included in emissions analysis. Two-day average bodyweights were collected at the beginning and end of the data collection period and were used to calculate final BW, BW gain, and average daily gain (ADG). Data were analyzed using ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey comparisons for animal performance and DMI (N = 26) and for methane emissions (N = 19). Sex was included as a fixed effect. No treatment x sex interactions were found (P > 0.05). Final BW (65.9±0.95kg), weight gain (7.8±0.49kg), ADG (0.2±0.07 kg/d), and DMI (75.8±3.30kg) were not affected by treatment or sex (P ≥ 0.16). Gain:feed was greater for HG (0.13±0.01) in comparison to HR (P = 0.01), with no difference observed between MIX (0.10±0.01) and HR (0.08±.01, P = 0.41). No differences were observed between HG and MIX (P = 0.09). Average daily methane emissions were greater (P ≤ 0.01) in HR (51.3gCH4/d) compared to MIX (47.2gCH4/d) and HG (40.4gCH4/d) lambs, but not different between MIX and HG (P = 0.23). Methane emissions relative to DMI (gCH4/kg DMI) were not different among treatments (P ≥ 0.27). These findings indicate that increasing GRR improves feed efficiency in finishing lambs with subtle effects on daily methane production. Additional research is warranted to fully elucidate the relationship between GRR and animal performance with respect to environmental sustainability across divergent sheep production systems.
